newsitem.title: USA: Weak Swiss franc sends dollar mostly higher before U.S. data.
newsitem.headline: Weak Swiss franc sends dollar mostly higher before U.S. data.

text.p: A weaker Swiss franc helped the dollar rise against European currencies Thursday as traders neutralised recent dollar sales before key data on the U.S. economy due on Friday.

The mark also fell against the dollar but rose to its highest level compared with the Swiss currency in 15-months amid renewed focus on Switzerland's weak economy and concern that an investigation into wartime deposits in Switzerland might lead to the suspension of its bank secrecy laws.

But markets should be thin with much of Europe closed on Friday, and dealers said they were keen to buy back some of the dollars sold Wednesday in case data on U.S. employment and the manufacturing sector produce adverse market swings.

"You had marks and Swiss sort of perky off and on through the course of the week," said Lisa Finstrom, currency analyst at Smith Barney Inc. "You've got a European holiday, where many of the centres are closed and you have a big U.S. number.
"So, I think there was a little bit of profit-taking on that and it just gathered a bit of momentum."
On Thursday, the dollar rose to 1.2680 Swiss francs from 1.2553 late Wednesday and to 1.5180 marks from 1.5114 marks.
The government releases its widely-anticipated report on October unemployment, along with September factory orders data Friday.
The market will also look to a key index of manufacturing activity from the National Association of Purchasing Management to confirm recent signs of a U.S. economic slowdown.
Strong data would increase the possibility of a Federal Reserve interest rate increase and could spook U.S. asset and currency markets.

Dealers attributed the Swiss franc's fall in part to a wire-service report stating that Switzerland seeks to accelerate the easing of bank secrecy laws to allow experts to review the fate of Jewish money and Nazi assets deposited there in the second World War.
But Finstrom said the Swiss bank secrecy laws -- long the foundation of Switzerland's investment appeal -- have been coming down for years.
Of equal importance, the Swiss franc has recently seen its historical role as a safe-haven currency erode, traders said.

"The Swiss franc market is focusing for the first time in a long time on fundamentals...because of low interest rates and because of the state of the economy," said Bill Marr, foreign exchange manager at Credit Commerciale de France. "A lot of its international appeal is not being adhered to."
Elsewhere, the dollar ended slightly off at 114.03 yen, compared to 114.13 yen as the Japanese currency extended recent gains against the mark.

"That is just a function of marks/yen," said Dennis Pettit, foreign exchange manager of Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan. "You saw ...selling pressure of (marks against yen), a continuation from yesterday."
The dollar closed at Canadian $1.3385, down from C$1.3413 on Wednesday. The pound fell after setting a 19-month high on Wednesday, closing at $1.6270, compared to $1.6330.
